questions.q: What does the `WITH STOPAT` clause do in a log restore?
options: Replays the transaction log only up to the specified date and time, discarding any transactions committed after that moment
Stops the entire restore chain and rolls it back completely
Pauses the restore until manually resumed
Restores only the most recent log backup, ignoring earlier ones
questions.explain: STOPAT lets SQL Server roll the log forward to an exact moment and stop there, as if later transactions never happened.

questions.q: In a full + differential + log restore chain, what is the correct order and RECOVERY pattern?
options: Full, then differential, then log backups in sequence — every step but the last uses NORECOVERY
Log backups first, then differential, then full — RECOVERY on every step
Any order is fine as long as WITH RECOVERY is used on the full backup
Differential first, then full, then logs, with NORECOVERY only on the full
questions.explain: The chain must be applied in the order the backups were taken, and only the final statement in the chain uses WITH RECOVERY.

questions.q: Why does point-in-time restore require FULL (or BULK_LOGGED) recovery rather than SIMPLE?
options: SIMPLE recovery truncates the log automatically, so there's no unbroken log backup chain to roll forward through
SIMPLE recovery doesn't support full backups
Point-in-time restore is a licensing feature unrelated to recovery model
FULL recovery is required by SQL Server for any restore of any kind
questions.explain: An unbroken log chain is required to roll forward to an arbitrary point, and SIMPLE recovery's automatic truncation prevents that chain from existing.

questions.q: What limitation does BULK_LOGGED recovery introduce for point-in-time restore, per this lesson?
options: If the target moment falls inside a minimally-logged bulk operation, SQL Server can't stop at an arbitrary point inside it
BULK_LOGGED prevents point-in-time restore entirely
BULK_LOGGED requires a differential backup before every log restore
BULK_LOGGED restores are always slower than FULL recovery restores
questions.explain: This is the same tradeoff introduced in Lesson 1 — BULK_LOGGED sacrifices precise point-in-time recovery through minimally-logged bulk operations.

questions.q: A restore chain has the full backup, the differential, and log backups 1 and 3 — but log backup 2 is missing. What happens if you try to STOPAT a time covered by log backup 3?
options: The restore fails — the chain is broken because log backup 3's LSN range can't connect to log backup 1 without log backup 2
SQL Server skips the missing log backup automatically and restores anyway
The restore succeeds because STOPAT only checks the final log backup, not the whole chain
The restore succeeds but silently loses only the transactions from the missing backup
questions.explain: Log backups must connect via unbroken LSN ranges. A gap anywhere in the sequence breaks the entire chain, regardless of which backup you're ultimately trying to restore to.
